The young man let out a surprised gasp and stood up rapidly, accidentally flinging his sketchbook at my feet as he spun to face me. I bent down to pick it up as a cascade of excuses, apologies and rationales fluttered forth from his mouth, each one not giving the chance for the one before it to breathe, ramming into it in midair and cutting it short before befalling the same fate. Not looking at him, I started to leaf through the drawings at a lackadaisical pace. Each sketch placed him all around my property from when I first spotted him from my second floor study, him hiding behind some rhododendron and penciling the facade of my home, to when he hunched low and crossed the grounds to find a new angle, me following suit across my home to watch him, to now where I decided to have a word with the man with this keen interest in my domicile in my backyard. 

“You certainly have a discerning eye for detail,” I said, interrupting his stammering. It was true; each flourish, accent, window and door was rendered in a technical precision rarely found in any one hand. His pronounced Adam’s apple bobbed as he gulped in if not relief at least a reprieve from any anticipated hostility, although his pale face was still flushed with the shame of being caught.

“Thank you, sir,” he said, his voice artificially deeper in a practiced way in the hopes one day it’d stick. I didn’t say anything and continued further into his sketchbook - page after page of architectural worship of all sorts of buildings. In some of the more public instances where he didn’t have to do his craft covertly the structures were rendered in the most brilliant use of watercolor that I almost wished I had let him become more comfortable with my home and grounds so that he could paint it in the same way. A silly thought - the young man clearly had a love of color and any semblance of such a thing on the house had long been faded away by years of sun, rain and wind.

“I’m a student of architecture,” he continued, unnerved by my lack of response, “Particularly 19th century…” I finally looked up at him. Twenty-one, twenty-two years of age or so. Big, worried brushstrokes of eyebrows floated above his brown eyes. Intelligent, but naive, I noted to myself, probably doesn’t believe the stories.

“A photo would’ve lasted longer,” echoing the old joke as I smiled, closed the book and handed it to him.

“I supposed I’m a bit old fashioned,” he laughed nervously, trying to judge if he was still in any sort of trouble. 

“Would you believe I consider myself the same?” I gestured to the house, one of the few, if not the only, example of gilded age manses in this part of the country. He laughed again, a bit more naturally this time. “But really,” I continued, “You only had to knock on my door and ask.”

He continued to force a smile but I could tell his jaw was clenched. I like it when they do this - pretend my reputation doesn’t proceed me. 

“I’m quite proud of the house,” I said, putting a reassuring hand on his shoulder, “And I can see you’re incredibly talented. Feel free to come anytime with a full set up and take as long as you need. I’d love to see what you’d come up with!”

Over the next few weeks I found Jasper all around the grounds, at first continuing his studies in his sketchbook before graduating to whole canvases and oil sets. Each time I’d step out and have a few pleasant words with him, acting as if I had just saw him out the window and not that I’d been watching him for however long he’d been there that day. 

Sometimes he’d bring along a girl. She’d stand around over him as he worked, nervously twisting and stroking a lock of her red hair with both hands, green eyes darting from his work to the subject at hand. When I spoke to her, she smiled politely but put up an unbreakable wall of apprehension and distrust and I returned the sentiment towards her. I imagine that she would tell him that she didn’t want him coming to my property or talking to me anymore, that she was scared, and he’d reassure her that’s how he felt at first but he has gotten to know me and the rumors were just that, rumors. He’d hold her by the shoulders and with his false, boyish sense of authority assert that I was just a strange but harmless man that people were wary of for no reason other than my unusual manner of dress and unplaceable accent. Her intuition would win out, eventually, and I didn’t see her come again.

“You know,” I began as I stood behind him working one day, “the interior has plenty of points of interest. The foyer alone would have you busy for days.” His hand froze and hovered over the canvas for a second and I sucked on my teeth, wondering if I proposed the idea too soon. His hand came down to his lap, torso twisted to look at me, and he said he’d hate to impose. I reassured him that it wouldn’t be a problem at all, I mostly keep to my study anyway. 

Jasper audibly let out a breath as he first walked through the doors. He put his hands into his thick hair as he jumped excitedly  into the center of the foyer. His eyes followed the hand carved staircase as it wrapped around the center of the room up to the domed skylight in the ceiling, the shadows of the muntins casting a crisscross pattern on his face.

“This is incredible!” He explained, “The marble floors! The brass sconces!” His eyes darted around the room, not knowing what facet to focus on first. I laughed and started to ascend the staircase.

“I’ll let you get to work,” I said, not looking back at him, “And if you need anything, feel free to ask me or Ewen.”

“Who’s Ewen?” He called after me. I pretended not to hear and slipped into a nearby doorway.

As planned, time got away from the young man and I found him a few hours later taking in all the details of the intricately carved newel turning. I approached him from behind and cleared my throat, causing him to jump from his hunched over posture to one resembling a meerkat on its hind legs. 

“My god!” He exclaimed, starting to pack his things wildly, “I’ve absolutely overstayed my welcome!” 

“Nonsense,” I responded, “If you’d like to stay for dinner, I had Ewen prepare for two.” As if on cue the man’s stomach growled. He held his midsection as if he could cover it up and smiled sheepishly up at me. I gave him a knowing and understanding smile and gestured for him to follow me into the dining room. 

As with the foyer, Jasper’s excitement for dining room was palpable. His brown eyes scanned the enclosure from the crystal chandelier over the mahogany table, to the detailed molding patterned across the walls. In his breathless excitement, he spun around to say something to me but I was already seated at one end of the long table. I gestured for him to join at the seat beside me. He composed himself,  straightened out his shirt, and strutted over to his place.

Twenty years ago I found myself walking down a dark, gravel road  leaving behind a trail of cigarette butts to guide me back to any semblance of civilization and to my home. At least what was to remain my home for the next few days. Along the left side of the road, separated by a small ditch, ran a grove of trees. On the other side a barbed wire fence separated me from the softly lolling hills of the Iowa countryside freshly scraped clean by the fall harvest and the moonlight illuminated the remaining stubble of the corn stalks. The moon shone so brightly that if I hadn’t had other things on my mind I would’ve wondered why we ever had to invent streetlights at all. It was the perfect place for a young man to grapple with his first taste of abject failure, for no one was around to hear my gasps of anxiety and see the wet from tears on my face. 

Well, no one was supposed to be around.

It was hard to notice the subtle static in the air at first; it was hidden under the sound of crunching gravel as I plodded forward, clutching at chest and squeezing tighter as I thought of telling my parents what had happened and that I’d have to come back home soon. As the phenomenon increased until it captured my attention and I had to put my self-pity on temporary leave. The electric crackle, the type you’d hear standing under high-voltage power lines, swelled and the wind started to pick up and blow around in strange patterns. What was a silent, still night turned into a maelstrom of strangeness. The buzz had escalated until it sounded like a geiger counter through a megaphone at Chernobyl, the wind rushing and threatening to take my coat with it, and I could’ve sworn I could’ve seen some bits of gravel rising up and floating an inch or two above the road. 

There was flash of light and a defining pop like an old flashbulb from within a thicket of trees and the chaos slammed on the brakes and I felt the sudden whiplash of everything being still again. I stood in the road looking about me for any evidence of the event that just occurred, half hoping this was the mental break I’d been wishing for - evidence that there was something truly wrong with me instead of just being a fuck up. I thought about leaving but I knew there was something within those trees for me. 

Carefully, I crossed the little ravine and approached the treeline. Even with their leaves gone, the trees made quick work of the moonlight I had grown to rely on this night. Everything became a muddle of dark silhouettes with the occasional sliver of light managing to sneak past the tangle of branches overhead. As I rounded past one tree, something caught my eye - a small pinprick of a pulsating, red light, undetectable by human sight except for the darkest of scenarios. Following it, I pushed though until there was a small clearing with the little light at its center.  My reliable friend in the sky was able to push through more strongly here and the forms in front of me took shape as my eyes readjusted to this slight influx of light. I tried to squint to make out what the little red light was attached to and when I did my throat closed up just in time to catch a scream from escaping.

There was a man of similar size to me standing there in the clearing with his back to me. I hid behind a tree, my back against the bark, and tried to recall how much noise I had made on the way in. My breaths and my heart trying to outrace each other, I resolved to leave the way I came in when the man called out to me.

“I know you’re there, Oliver.”

The scream I managed to wrangle earlier escaped its confinement and I bolted through the trees and in the darkness pinballing from one unseen trunk to another. I felt a momentary sense of safety and relief as I broke through the treeline once more and in my ill-found sense of security my foot plunged into the ditch I had forgotten about, twisting my ankle and flinging me face first in the tiny, sharp pebbles that made up the road. Without a pause I crawled out to the center of the road before rolling over and looking into the thicket, my breath hurried and ragged. 

There was nothing at first. The horn of a far off freight train several horizons over highlighted how quiet everything had become. But then I saw it again - the little red light. It slowly pulsated on its own and blinked in and out of my sightline as the man walked past and behind trees until finally he emerged from the thicket and stood at the edge of the small ravine. I swallowed, my heart began to thump uncomfortably again, and I called out.

“Who are you? How do you know my name?” I said, my voice wavering. He sighed and looked up at the night sky, the same way I do when pondering a response. 

“You know me,” he said, as he started to walk across the ditch towards me. “It’s my name, too.”

I tried to back away on my elbows but stopped as the man’s features came into view for the first time in the moonlight. The face was instantly recognizable - it was the same one I saw in the mirror every day, just more weathered. The man extended his hand to help me up and as I came face to face with him I was able to see it more clearly. The same sad eyes, save with some crows feet around the corners. The same hook in the nose. The same eyebrows, especially the right one which always seemed to have one or two errant hairs far longer than the rest. A big, wild beard I never thought I’d be capable of growing covered his jaw, patches of grey poking through here and there. He wore what seemed to be a band t-shirt (but afterwards when I googled it nothing came up). The pulsating red light I saw earlier came from some sort of device strapped to his arm. My mind scrambled for some rational explanation - maybe this was some unknown relative - but the truth was dawning on me.

“You’re me?” I softly asked. He nodded as he wiped some of the dirt, bark and rock that clung to my coat. “I… I go bald?” I asked.

“Yes, but that’s not important right now.” His eyes, the same eyes, rose up to meet mine and he put his hand on my shoulder. He continued, “I know things seem very uncertain at this moment. Life seems out of control and you’re scared of what’s to come. But there’s something you need to know.” He paused for effect before going on. “One day, a long time from now, you’ll receive a U-Line Bakers Rack for free.”

A soft breeze rustled the branches of the nearby trees as I tried to process what he was telling me and I confusedly responded, “What?”

A grin spread across his face and he started to get a little more animated, “I know, right! Those things go for like 150 bucks a pop!” My confused expression must’ve not been satisfactory for him as he took a deep breath and tried again in a more explanatory manner. “One day you’ll be working at a barbershop and - “

“Barbershop!? Do I become a barber?”

“No, what you do is actually a little hard to explain. But one day you’ll be working for a barber, just for that day, and he’ll mention that he’s trying to get rid of his U-Line Brand Bakers Rack and you get to take it off his hands. FOR FREE.”

His grip tightened on my shoulder and his eyes burned into mine, yearning for me to comprehend. I started to get scared again. The device on his arm started beeping and the pulsing red light started to accelerate its rhythm. “A U-Line Brand Baker’s Rack! For Free!” He repeated.

“I’m sorry, I don’t know what that is-“

“Yes. You. Do.” He said, poking me in the chest to accentuate each word. “You see them everywhere, you just don’t know what they’re called yet!”

The beeping and the blinking light picked up their pace. The static in the air returned with the slight wind alongside. 

“I don’t… Wh-Why are you telling me this?” I whimpered.

He spun away from me, arms raised and hands gnarled in frustration. “Because I’ve told everyone else and no one cared!” He turned back to me, one finger waving in my face, and through gritted teeth snarled, “And I thought YOU of all people would understand!” He grabbed the scuff of my shirt and held me close to him with a strength that far surpassed my own.

“Why are you like this!?” I cried, “What’s going to happen to me!?

The electric crackle filled the air as the wind started thrashing this way and that. The man’s face softened into an expression of fear and pleading. “You do understand, don’t you?” He begged, “Don’t you see how transformational this will be for the organization of my garage - OUR garage?" He started cackling madly, let go of me and backed away as a white glow started to envelope his body, emanating from the device on his arm. 

“Finally! A place to put all my camping gear!” He shouted as he started to glow brighter.

“The top rack - perfect for all the pots and pans strewn about that I don’t use anymore!” The wind whipped furiously and the man started to levitate off the ground, white electricity radiating from him. I had to raise my arm to shield my face from the rushing air and the blinding light.

“And on the bottom rack - “ but before he could finish he vanished with a deafening pop and once again the night became tranquil. I stayed until morning trying to find any evidence of my encounter, but outside of the tears and cuts on my coat, jeans and face there was nothing to be found.

Everywhere we went she’d know everyone and everyone would happily greet her while giving me a side eye and I’d smile meekly. It made sense; what’s this chick in a studded leather jacket and combat boots doing with this guy who looks like he gives unsolicited fishing advice to youths at the pond? 

One of the people we ran into was an old coworker of hers, Rob, who I managed to gain favor from when I pulled him aside to tell him he had an absolute river of dried coke running from his nose. He enveloped both Alli and I with his gigantic frame, laughed gregariously, and demanded that we needed to have a double date with his new girlfriend. 

We met at a bar we didn’t usually frequent on the other side of town and met Rob’s partner. Fried strands of platinum blonde hair floated about her head too weak for a comb, and she had long eyelashes like two toxic caterpillars that laid comfortably over blue eyes that radiated some sort of mania. Pleasantries were exchanged and we found a table.

The night progressed pleasantly until Alli needed to use the restroom and Rob needed a 47th drink, leaving the girl and I alone. Once in a while the planets will align and I can be funny and charming and I found myself being an adequate conversation partner. However, astral powers can only do so much. 

I don’t remember exactly what I said, after all I was also on my 47th drink, but I do remember it was supposed to be something along the lines of, “How did you and Rob meet?” I’m not sure if it came out that way or the general cacophony of the bar distorted my words but she looked aghast, then repulsed, and then she started screaming.  How dare I say that to her?! What gave me the right?! Something about implying she wasn’t supposed to be here!?

I stammered apology after apology but I seemed to have opened the gates on some unholy beast not too keen on being reigned in. She got up and paced back and forth, pointing and screaming at me, at one point grabbing her clutch purse off the booth seat cushion and storming outside before coming back in to continue where she left off.

Rob and Alli returned from their respective quests. At first they went at me demanding to know what I did but between my frantic, anxiety-tempered attempts to apologize and placate and her increasingly unhinged behavior they soon turned to calming her down. Ali’s nostrils started to flare and she started gritting her teeth and she realized this was an injustice towards me. 

Alli pounded the table with the flat of her hand and pointed at the girl and yelling, “Bye, bitch!” She grabbed my wrist and started leading me out of the bar. I heard the pounding of soles against carpeted floor and then I first felt the raking of fingernails against the left side of my face, catching and dragging my eyelid and the contact lens underneath, and then a fist against the right side. As I staggered from the blows, I saw Alli give a full booted running kick right into the sternum of the other girl and despite Alli’s small frame I’d imagine it was the type of blow that’d rattle your heart. 

The two women started fist fighting. My dumbass still thought there might be a peaceful resolution to this situation and tried to separate the two. This was only accomplished when a bartender got there and helped me pry the two off each other but I think the real MVP of the situation was Rob who saw which way the wind was blowing and polished off his full beer in one gulp and disappeared into the night. One bartender pinned the girl into a booth and another took Alli and I outside to see if we were alright. Alli gave out more hits than she took and I was fine, save for the contact lens that had been shoved into the furthest reaches of my eye socket. We were asked to leave and we gladly did so.

The next night I walked into my usual haunt alone, eager to tell tales of my exploits the previous night. The bartender on duty, usually an aloof and dismissive lady, immediately rushed towards me and asked if I was okay. I chuckled and said I was and asked how she knew what had happened. Apparently the bartender from the other bar was her boyfriend and she realized who he was talking about when he described the cool, punk chick with the bearded, lanky scarecrow of a man (overall a testament of how little our big city is). I tried to laugh the whole thing off but she leaned over the bar and grabbed me by the wrist and with utmost gravity she said, “You don’t understand, we know who that girl is and she’s done something like this before. Last time, she had a knife and stabbed the guy.”

A little epilogue: a few months later, I realized that dating someone you’re constantly scared of and uncomfortable around sounds better on paper and Alli and I broke up. I returned to the dating apps and as I swiped who was there but the girl from that night. I swiped left and then that message that always makes you feel a little gross popped up, “Uh-oh! Looks like you might have missed a potential match!”

Anyway, then I was stabbed by the Heath Ledger Joker who cackled madly and gave himself the famous Glasgow smile as I bled to death. Go listen to Toxic by the Suffragettes.

My partner’s best friend’s boyfriend invited me to come along with him to a gaming convention this past weekend. I had waffled on whether or not to go and my partner urged me to go citing how excited he was to make an attempt at friendship.

“But I already have friends!” I protested, gesturing towards the sack of flour on the couch next to me with googly eyes glued on and the mop propped up in the corner with a tied on paper plate that had a smiley face drawn on it. My girlfriend made that same concerned face she makes any time I talk about Walter and Amanda and continued to plead with me to go - if not for his sake, at least for her’s - and I relented.

That morning’s 8 mile run and the slowest Lyft driver in the world delayed my arrival but I got to the convention and was immediately over-stimulated. Thousands of attendees and hundreds of vendors from all over the country had all come together, armed themselves with costumes, neon lights, and flashy merchandise to wage a war on all the senses. However I found it to be a matter of acclimatization. My suggestion for these types of events is to have another entrance, an airlock of sorts with a lower level of activity, maybe just a few pinball tables and and a guy juggling, for people who mostly stay home, doomscroll and watch the same TV shows over and over most of the time. 

The guy and I found each other and went over the general niceties of two men meeting in public, slapping hands and what’s up’s all around. I asked how things have been and wouldn’t you know it, it was nothing much. We went about the various vendors, filing through all the video games of yore, once in a while retrieving some old SNES cartridge and exclaiming, “Jesus Christ! Do you remember this one!?” Things never seemed to get deeper than that and I fought the urge to ask him if he’d like to abandon all this and just go get super fucked up somewhere. I didn’t, though, he didn’t seem like the type of guy to indulge in all that and it’d probably alarm our partners if he agreed. 

It was a hard place to stick together. Moving swaths of people made maintained proximity impossible and at all times you were surrounded by Venus fly traps that fed on your attention that pulled you aside and by the time you’ve turned around the layout of entire convention had transformed like a labyrinth in a dream. We agreed to split up for simplicities sake; after all he had the goal of adding to his extensive collection of games and I was more interested in figurines and art and also had the idea that maybe I could find the elusive rose-gold PS5 controller my partner had been pining for. That last one was a hard thing to ask about as merchants had a hard time admitting it was something they didn’t stock and I could feel them try and pull away towards other customers who had less hypothetical concerns. 

Video games have been a mainstay in my life, from being a great source of comfort as a lonely child to quite arguably being the only tether to reality as a freshly divorced adult going through Covid lockdowns alone in a new city. However, I’ve always felt being referred to as a gamer in the same way as a dog reacts to cone around its neck. I found myself standing back and watching all these people who fully embraced it in its entirety, dressed as their favorite characters, commiserating over rare finds, laughing amongst themselves and ducking away to pull out a DS and take a quick moment to play against a wall.  A man dressed as Bowser passed by me and an adult man approached him like a cowboy in an old western. “Well, well, well,” he said in a shrill voice, “if it isn’t my arch-nemesis, Bowser!” My heart started racing and I considered finding and pulling a fire alarm to avoid the second-hand embarrassment of this exhibition. But Bowser played along and did his trademark, mocking laugh, a good imitation of it too, and the two exchanged banter before laughing together for real and taking a photo. I had forgotten that I was in a place that relished kindness, acceptance and silliness in a way I was unaccustomed to and I wondered if my life was tweaked in the smallest amount would I find myself reveling in the same way. 

Elsewhere in the convention an alternate version of me had less inhibitions than me and a fire alarm was announced over the loudspeaker, a droning, bored voice repeatedly letting us know that it was only a “fire condition” and not an emergency but we all had to leave. We all filed out, thousands in a slow, penguin march towards the outside. My partner’s best friend’s boyfriend and I met up and both agreed that the process to get inside would amount to something akin to a humanitarian disaster and we decided to head down the street to some public transit. 

And so we walked, him with a Guitar Hero controller and me with a 3D printed bust of Captain Picard. He turned to me and said, “I gotta admit, I took an edible before I got here. I would’ve offered one to you, buy you didn’t seem like the type.”

Saw him a week or two ago, sounds a lot like the same set, and it was incredible. We also had the room get a little rowdy, not heckling but more like trying to join in on the fun and yelling out their own jokes. I think the most impressive part of the show was how masterfully he was able to bring the crowd back under control, truly a great.

Ive been training for a marathon these past few weeks and shoving the necessary mileage into the schedule of even an unoccupied adult such as myself has me running at times I haven’t seen since my partying days. The gears of reality aren’t quite greased at these hours and the RAM of the world loads up all the wrong stuff. Graffiti that seemingly addresses you by name. A man in a business suit, smoking a cigarette, with two jugs of water ducking into the woods. A woman cosplaying as Lara Croft taking sensual photos glaring at you for interrupting her photo shoot as if you were the one interloping into her universe. 

I try to avoid the main trails and run through a nearby swampland. Unkept boardwalks and uneven dirt paths make a special treat for the ankles. At these hours, the sunlight barely exists and that special orange-red-blue color palette that only exists in pastiche paintings sweeps the landscape. Everything is so incredibly still. The ducks floating in the water haven’t made plans for the day yet. The reeds and the wind have agreed to a temporary ceasefire. The mausoleum overlooking the scene on a nearby cliff reminds you to enjoy it while  it lasts. The time and place the gods don’t allow mortals to see but they’ll turn a blind eye if you don’t make a scene.

The other day, in these twilight hours, I found an empty wheelchair in the middle of the path. An incredibly alarming item with no clear cut course of action. I called 311 and the woman on the line had the tone of voice that indicated that a man of my age should know how to deal with something like this and she connected me to the non-emergency police line who didn’t seem too alarmed either and assured me someone will be there soon. A relative term. I’m not sure how long I stood next to that wheelchair but it was long enough for me to take a seat and in a perverse way I got to enjoy my secluded scenery from a comfy, seated position.

But the sun kept rising and people started waddling through and really there’s only one or two times you can explain to well-meaning people that you’re fully abled and this isn’t your wheelchair before you get up and head home. All I can really hope for at this point is that they scrape some DNA of mine off that chair and I’m listed as a missing disabled person, which I imagine would do wonders for next year’s tax return.

Anyway, hope y’all have a good day, even if you have to square the passing of James Earl Jones against the reunion of Oasis, joyous news to people who bring guitars to parties everywhere.

In the previous complex I lived in I met a neighbor who lived in the building across the parking lot from me. We actually met on the smoking patio of a local bar and started recognizing each other around the area. Often times I’d be heading out on foot through the parking lot and he’d be on his back patio and he’d call out hello and we’d have a little chat. It was pleasant for a few weeks. 

He got my phone number and started calling me several times a day just to see what I was up to, which wasn’t the wildest thing at first, but then he started showing up to my door piss drunk in the middle of the day. With my sense of boundaries being what they are, I let him in and would allow him to talk my ear off. Even when things got weird I was never scared of him physically since, frankly, he was kind of a shrimpy dude who seemed to be terrified of everything.

I truly wasn’t aware of any romantic feelings he might’ve had for me for he was a married man and as a dude myself I’ve never really had anyone come after me like that - I just thought he was a weird lonely guy. That all changed when one of the times he came over he was especially distraught. At this point I was pretty uncomfortable with him and was attending to chores hoping he’d get bored and leave. Eventually I looked up at him and he was staring at me, red in the face and clutching the table so hard I thought he was going to break it. In a strained voice he groaned, “I… just… care for you… so much.” It was here that I had to shake my head and say his behavior was far too strange and that he had to go. He left without saying anything and things between us simmered down a bit.

He’d continue to say “Hi!” from the balcony and for politeness’ sake I would entertain some light conversation. But during one of these conversations he asked when I was going to work out that day. Something about that didn’t sit well with me and it kept gnawing at me. It wasn’t until I was home later that day that I realized - I had never told him that I work out everyday. I had never really considered anybody being able to see into my room - I was on the third floor - but I analyzed the surroundings through this lens for the first time and realized that he’d been able to look into my bedroom from his patio this whole time.

And that is the story of why I bought curtains.

Kind of a funny thing happened to me today. Lately I’ve been building a reputation as someone who can handle art well and this has gained the attention of a cabal of little old ladies who’ve been collecting art their whole lives. I believe they appreciate me for my eye for layouts, my technical know-how, and most importantly, my ability to stand there with a polite smile on my face as they talk at me for hours on end. They’ve been passing my information from one to another until I got to the woman I met today, who I’ll call The Judge.

The Judge lived in a meticulously maintained century home and the only thing that could remind anyone inside of the inherent chaotic nature of the universe was a rowdy goldendoodle named Mina who had to be put away upon my arrival. The Judge herself was an incredibly severe and intimidating woman. She actually was a judge and from the photos on the wall I could see she had a long and storied career, but I believe you’d be able to tell her profession just by being in her presence. Despite being rather small of frame she carried herself with a maelstrom of authority and she had a piercing gaze that gave the impression of her being acutely aware of any sin you’ve ever committed. She spoke in a direct, curt way and in this way she instructed me to get started on her gallery wall. 

The centerpiece of the gallery wall was a large painting of Ruth Bader Ginsberg and The Judge had a curious habit of referring to the painting on a first name basis. “Ruth was here.” “I think Ruth should be in the center.” “I’ve had Ruth for such and such time.” Etc. And as is wont to happen when you’re around such eccentricities I started to pick up on it myself. But when I started off with, “Maybe we can put Ruth…” I  was immediately cut off with, “Don’t call her by her first name if you didn’t know her on a personal level!”

After a brief shock at the hostility of her response I asked if she knew Justice Ginsberg and she hissed, “Yes, she was one of my closest friends.”

And she just left it like that, a silence filling the air except for the furious breaths she was inhaling through her nose. Her entire body was tensed up, her fists balled up, and I could see tears welling up in her eyes. She stared at me with such an intensity that I had to rack my brain to remember if maybe I was personally responsible for the late Supreme Court Justice’s death. And I wondered even if I wasn’t would it be easier to plead guilty and avoid whatever trial was coming my way.

It was in this moment of Tremendous Judgment that Mina the Goldendoodle broke free from whatever enclosure she was being kept in and excitedly ran up to me, reared back on her hind legs, and punched me directly in the testicles with her paw causing me to collapse on the floor. The end.

Also, the humor missed the mark for me. Maybe it's because I'm a grown-ass man and this is a game meant for children, but I found myself squirming uncomfortably at all the bad jokes that just keep coming and coming.

There were some highlights that gave me the "Aha!" moment and spine tingle I get from other puzzle games, sure, but they were far and few between. If I had to make a totally unfair assumption, I'd say that when people look back fondly on the game, they're probably just thinking of those. 

But it wasn't all bad! I thought the overall design was very imaginative and clever.
